extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, creative-writing students, and readers evaluating whether a text is poetry or prose
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to identify, craft, and evaluate poetry (especially free verse) versus prose, focusing on poetic elements, rhythm, meter, form, and the balance of meaning and sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose: prose vs. poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prose is communication; poetry is art." The essential purpose of prose is to communicate ideas, while the essential purpose of poetry is to move us with the beauty of its crafted language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reader is moved by prose, he is moved primarily by its meaning. Poetry's aim is aesthetic effect; however, the author qualifies this by noting meaning is also important in poetry. Distinguish works primarily by whether they prioritize communication of information (prose) or crafted musical language (poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of meaning and sound in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry both meaning and sound are important; "the art of a poem should further its meaning." A great poem combines cogent meaning with musical language that advances the meaning with its sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem with lovely language that says nothing original or important is a failure (if written for an audience). Evaluate poems for how effectively musical language and sonic techniques enhance and deepen the poem's meaning—look for the 'double-whammy' of content + sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience matters: standards differ for private vs public poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry written only for one's self has no standards; standards apply when a poem is written for an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply strict evaluative standards to purely private exercises; criticism in this article is directed at poems intended for public readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory of poetic tools/elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's tools include: "metaphor, simile, parallelism, line breaks, enjambment, alliteration, consonance, assonance, form (stanzas, sonnets, etc.), rhythm, meter, internal rhyme, and end rhyme."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these devices to craft the poem's sound and structure; absence of most of these elements (beyond line breaks) is a signal the piece may be prosaic rather than poetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm as the key distinguisher
rubrics_metrics.description: "More than any other quality, rhythm distinguishes poetry from prose." Prose has a loose, undefined rhythm (emphases every 2nd–10th syllable), while poetry receives emphasis more frequently (every 1st–4th syllable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze cadence and stress patterning. The article gives examples contrasting prose cadence and poetic cadence and uses MacLeish's 'Ars Poetica' to show how rhythm operates even in free verse. Lack of a perceivable poetic rhythm is a mark of prosaic verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter's role: structure and momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter "is what gives a poem its structure and momentum; it carries the reader forward to the poem's conclusion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter can be informal and accessible (Frost, Auden, Roethke). Especially for longer poems, meter sustains coherence; evaluate whether a poem's meter (or echo of meter) provides forward motion. Metered poetry generally requires more technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and meaning interact (tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form of the poem creates imperatives in language and the meaning creates imperatives; the way the two interact creates tension. Removing form removes that tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of poetic form as a 'girdle' into which meaning is poured—the fit of meaning into form creates artistic energy. Assess how well the poem's formal constraints shape and enhance its content rather than merely accommodating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line breaks are necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Line breaks alone don't make poetry. Many contemporary free-verse pieces use line breaks but otherwise read like prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether line breaks are chosen for poetic effect (enjambment, sound, rhythm) or merely to make the line 'appear even'. Examples (Zulauf, Sirowitz) show pieces that rely only on line breaks and lack other poetic elements—these are prosaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound devices (alliteration, assonance, consonance, rhyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective poetry uses sound devices such as alliteration, assonance, consonance, internal rhyme, and end rhyme (in addition to rhythm and meter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey the poem for deliberate sonic techniques. MacLeish's 'Ars Poetica' is highlighted for rhythm, alliteration, assonance, rhyme (internal and end), and line breaks chosen for effect; such devices contribute to its poetic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and substantive content
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should 'advance our understanding of the world or ourselves'—poetry that says nothing original or important is a failure when aimed at an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poem offers fresh insight, credible emotion, or meaningful observations rather than empty or clichéd sentiments. Sound without substantive thought is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosaic free-verse pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosaic free verse—free verse that lacks most poetic elements except line breaks—tends to devolve into prose and 'misses the point of poetry altogether.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for loose rhythm, mundane diction, absence of soundcraft and imagistic intensity, and reliance on sentimentality. The article argues such poems are often produced by writers who lack a love of the sound of poetry and can be written by anyone; treat such works skeptically as poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of free verse vs. metered verse by length/function
rubrics_metrics.description: Free verse is a good choice for short, lyrical, intense or moody poems and for heavily rhythmic poetry (e.g., Whitman); but for longer works, the structure of meter is really needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match form to intention and length. For sustained long poems, expect formal underpinnings (meter or strong rhythmic strategy) to maintain integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craftsmanship and technical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Metered poetry generally takes more skill to write; well-crafted metered poetry is harder and tends to be more durable historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the technical demands of form when evaluating craft. The author cites many canonical poets who wrote in meter and argues posterity favors skillful practitioners; technical mastery increases a poem's lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of emotion and realistic grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poets develop emotions within the context of realistic events that people can relate to; avoid 'grand and phony sentiments' and self-congratulatory posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether emotional statements arise from credible particulars rather than from abstract, pompous, or condescending generalities. The critique of A.R. Ammons exemplifies how sentimentality can undermine poetic authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use form (stanzas, sonnets, sections) to enhance meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Form—stanzas, sonnet structures, sectional divisions—can be used intentionally to organize thought and sound; MacLeish's 'Ars Poetica' is noted for sectioned form that reinforces its effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether formal choices (couplets, sections, stanza breaks) contribute to the poem's musical and semantic architecture rather than being arbitrary ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion and revision as craft practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The author describes counting syllables and using scansion during composition: a line or group of lines may come in and then be scanned and sometimes rewritten in a different meter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat scansion and deliberate metrical revision as part of the poet's toolkit; evaluate drafts and final lines for evidence of attentive metrical shaping or intentional rhythmic choices.
